Patient-reported symptoms:

  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Margaret Chen

Margaret Chen was forty-two when a delivery truck ran a red light and struck the passenger side of her sedan. She had been driving home from a community outreach event—the kind of work she had done for fifteen years as a social ministry worker, coordinating support services for low-income families in the city's northeast parishes. The impact came without warning. One moment she was turning onto Maple Street; the next, the truck's grille filled her peripheral vision and the world became noise and metal and the sensation of her body no longer being her own. She was conscious through all of it: conscious of the car folding around her, conscious of her arm pinned against the door frame, conscious of not being able to move or stop what was happening to her.

The police report noted that the truck driver had not even attempted to brake. The report also noted that Margaret had been driving at the posted speed limit, in her lane, with the light in her favor. Nothing she had done caused the crash. Nothing she could have done would have prevented it. And yet, in the months that followed, Margaret came to understand her body as fundamentally unreliable—not because of her injuries, which were significant but ultimately healed, but because it had betrayed her by being in that car at that moment, moving in that direction, vulnerable to forces entirely beyond her control. She had come to believe that her own body could not be trusted to keep her safe, that something essential inside her had broken on impact and never fully mended.

For the first three weeks after discharge, Margaret tried to return to work. She had been scheduled to lead a workshop on accessing mental health resources. She sat in her office—a small converted storage room in the basement of St. Catherine's Church—and found that her hands shook when she tried to type. More troubling was the way her mind now worked: she could not relax, could not let her guard down, because relaxation felt like surrender, like an invitation for something terrible to happen. When she tried to sit quietly for even a few minutes, her chest would tighten and her breathing would shallow. It was as though her body was telling her that safety required constant vigilance, that any moment of peace was a moment when disaster could strike. So she stopped trying to rest. She filled her evenings with tasks—organizing files, preparing materials, anything to remain in motion, in control.

The avoidance came gradually. Within two months, Margaret had stopped driving altogether. She told herself it was temporary, a reasonable precaution while she adjusted. But as weeks became months, the thought of being in a vehicle—whether driving or as a passenger—generated such acute dread that she simply could not do it. Her colleagues began to notice that she was no longer attending off-site meetings. When they offered rides, she declined with vague excuses. The truth was that the image of cars hitting other cars had become intrusive and unbidden; she would see it when she closed her eyes, see it in the moment before she fell asleep. The idea of placing herself in a vehicle felt like volunteering for re-traumatization.

Her work began to suffer. The social ministry position required occasional travel to partner agencies across the city. By the nine-month mark, Margaret's supervisor had gently suggested that her reduced availability was affecting her ability to fulfill her role. Rather than explain the true source of her limitations—which felt shameful, inexplicable, as though she were being held hostage by her own mind—Margaret requested a reduction to part-time hours. She worked from the office now, coordinating by phone and email, her world contracting to the rooms she could reach on foot.

The hypervigilance had become a constant companion. She scanned for exits the moment she entered any space, even familiar ones. She startled at ordinary sounds—a door slamming, a car backfiring in the street outside, the unexpected ring of a telephone—her body launching into fight-or-flight before her conscious mind could catch up. What frightened her most was the feeling that she could not trust her own judgment about safety. Even when colleagues or her therapist from the initial crisis counseling told her that she was safe, that the risk of another accident was statistically low, she could not believe them. Her body held a different truth: that the world was dangerous, that she was vulnerable, and that nothing—not statistics, not careful driving, not the reassurances of others—could change that fundamental reality.

Now, at forty-eight, Margaret has been living with these constraints for six years. She has not driven since the accident. She has not been a passenger in a car in almost as long. She still works part-time, still helps people, but increasingly from behind a desk. She has not dated in years; the thought of being dependent on someone else for transportation, or of explaining why she cannot go anywhere, feels impossible. What brought her finally to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she realized she could not remember the last time she had felt safe—truly safe, not just the absence of immediate danger, but a sense that her body and her world were trustworthy. She sat in her apartment on a Tuesday evening and understood that she was no longer living a life; she was managing a disaster that had already passed. She is hoping that someone can help her understand why her mind will not let her move forward, why the unfairness of that single moment continues to hold her captive, and whether it is possible to ever trust her own body again.

missing_explanations: The vignette acknowledges that Margaret was not at fault ('Nothing she had done caused the crash. Nothing she could have done would have prevented it') and later references 'the unfairness of that single moment,' but there is no explicit description of her sense that nothing has been done about the injustice, no mention of lack of accountability, legal action, or her perception that the situation remains unresolved. The patient-reported symptom includes both components: (1) that what happened was unfair AND (2) that nothing has been done about it. While unfairness is touched on, the second component—the sense of unresolved accountability or lack of action taken—is absent from the vignette.
